question: When Intel is supply constrained, will customers wait, return later, or adopt alternatives? What supports DCAI margin durability after capacity relief?

conclusion.answer: Public customer evidence supports a segmented outcome. Certification, live-migration restrictions, large-memory requirements, specialized instructions and costly operational changes can retain some Intel workloads. Cloud-native buyers have demonstrated large migrations and built infrastructure that makes subsequent architecture changes easier. Shortages can therefore finance durable rival adoption, while multiarchitecture deployment also leaves a route back to x86. Neither permanent customer loss nor automatic return is established.
conclusion.largest_model_gap: Recurring demand for compute is not the same as recurring Intel sockets, and Intel sockets are not the same as a 40% DCAI operating margin. None of the customer sources reviewed discloses enough Intel CPU volume, negotiated price, unit manufacturing cost or segment mix to underwrite that long-run margin.
conclusion.confidence_scope: High confidence in the described technical and procurement mechanisms; no quantified population-wide switching rate, win probability, or 2027 customer wait-time prediction.
conclusion.most_decisive_followup: Observe repeat paid Xeon deployments and stable mix-adjusted economics after alternate capacity is available. A launch, partnership or compatibility claim alone does not answer the duration question.

method.selection: Purposive mechanism sample, not a statistical sample of Intel customers. Prioritized named production workloads and buyer engineering accounts; included counterexamples to both universal stickiness and universal interchangeability.
limits: Vendor case studies are selected success stories. Buyer engineering accounts still select successful projects and do not report the full procurement alternatives.
Historical migration results do not directly predict behavior during a prospective 2027 shortage.
Current dynamic documentation was checked on the as-of date; it can change.
No interviews, private orders, confidential pricing or new outreach were used.
Cloud price/performance and end-user savings do not identify CPU manufacturer profit.

locators: Verifying instance availability and deploying to production

observations: By year-end 2023, roughly 2,000 services representing 70% of AWS workloads had migrated to Arm; Datadog reports a 10% AWS bill reduction.
Teams built dual-architecture images and validated dependencies, performance and capacity. Some services were excluded for degraded performance or missing specialized instance shapes.
Graviton3 scarcity required x86 fallback. Some migrations spanned multiple quarters.
cases.status: Actual production migration; not merely availability or recommendation.
cases.inference: Initial porting is costly, but its output is a reusable option to allocate across architectures. Capacity scarcity can trigger substitution. A later return to x86 remains technically possible, though Intel must earn it economically.
limits: AWS workloads are not all Datadog infrastructure.
The source does not identify the x86 fallback vendor, so this is not proof of Intel retention.
Cloud bill savings are not CPU chip-cost savings.
cases.model_use: Support a contestable workload bucket and distinguish first-time migration cost from ongoing allocation friction.

locators: Applying Learnings to Design OCI A4 Instances from Silicon to System

observations: Uber describes 24 months of joint work with OCI and Ampere after its 2023 cloud transition began. Experience on A1/A2 informed A4 silicon and configurations.
Early Arm adoption exposed cross-socket, cache, garbage-collection and single-thread performance problems. Gurobi-based services were slower on A1 than existing x86.
A4 development targeted higher-frequency options, cache and workload-specific memory configurations.
cases.status: Actual earlier-generation production use and coengineering; not a quantified A4 purchase contract.
cases.inference: Rival adoption can become a multi-generation engineering relationship. Intel can retain workload niches, but evidence of an old rival weakness is not proof that the weakness persists.
limits: Existing x86 vendor is unspecified.
No binding duration, purchased chips, prices or share of total fleet is disclosed here.
Coengineering is stronger evidence than a catalog listing but weaker than contracted revenue.
cases.model_use: Require workload-specific evidence for enduring advantage and track whether competing generations solve the cited bottleneck.

observations: Odin spans approximately five million cores across on-premises/cloud and x86/Arm. Performance-aware allocation was rolling out across about 1.4 million automatically scaled cores.
For Kafka, the newest cloud x86 factor is 196 versus 127 for newest Arm, a 1.54x ratio.
Production data required revisions to synthetic benchmark factors; Kafka and Cassandra differed. Kafka allocated cores fell about 8%.
cases.inference: Recurring workload demand can coexist with vendor-neutral scheduling and fewer required cores. Buyers seek delivered service capacity, not a constant number of nominal cores.
limits: CPU models, vendor identity of x86, contracts and prices are undisclosed.
Do not attribute the 1.54x difference to Intel or treat it as a universal benchmark.
An allocated core is not a newly purchased CPU.
cases.model_use: Normalize forecast demand by workload performance and utilization before translating it into manufacturer units.

observations: Amadeus reports 90% of its shopping engine on Cobalt100; the separate 95% figure refers to production workloads on Azure, not Arm share.
It first used Ampere in production in early 2024, then Cobalt in December2024.
The first C++ port required recompilation and extensive validation. Ampere-to-Cobalt required no recompilation.
The case reports roughly 20% throughput improvement and 8% response-time improvement.
cases.status: Actual critical production deployment; further Java/Couchbase exploration is prospective.
cases.inference: A mission-critical recurring service need not remain x86-bound. Once the architecture migration cost is paid, changing suppliers within Arm may be easier.
limits: Selected Microsoft success story.
Not a controlled comparison with current Intel/AMD alternatives; no CPU procurement economics.
cases.model_use: Avoid treating enterprise criticality alone as an Intel moat.

source.date_note: Publication date not displayed or found in retrieved metadata; current page checked 2026-11-05.

observations: Toyota describes SAP supporting 14 North American facilities and approximately 30,000 employees, with database size rising from 6TB in 2020 to 24TB in 2024.
It refreshed earlier Intel U-1 instances with U7i/R6i. Coordinated facility downtime, testing and controls checks preceded migration in under two weeks.
The narrative says R8i/R8i-flex/X8i are being evaluated.
cases.status: Actual Intel-to-Intel refresh; newest Xeon6 adoption is not established by the body.
cases.inference: Operational change risk, certification and memory scale can make incumbent refresh economically attractive. This is a concrete retention mechanism, not proof customers accept indefinite supply delays.
limits: Title/overview claim Xeon6; body names U7i/R6i and only future evaluation of Xeon6.
No negotiated price, committed volume or guaranteed future choice.
cases.model_use: Supports a sticky enterprise bucket, conditional on certified availability and total ownership economics.

generation_checks.fact: U7i uses fourth-generation Intel Xeon Scalable processors, not Xeon6.
R6i uses third-generation Intel Xeon Scalable processors.

sources.locator: FAQ: why AMD-based VM families are not certified for SAP HANA

sources.type: CSP announcement with named SAP executive quotation

sources.locator: Separate SAP HANA and Business Suite/NetWeaver lists

observations: Azure documentation states AMD is unsupported for SAP HANA, including virtualized scenarios. Lenovo separately lists Intel for HANA and AMD for Business Suite/NetWeaver.
SAP HANA Cloud, a managed service, has supported Graviton since November2023. SAP reports continued work through Graviton5 in June2026.
cases.status: Current certification boundary plus actual managed-service architecture adoption; not all SAP products have the same hardware requirements.
cases.inference: Certification can protect a specific installed workload without protecting all future spending in that software ecosystem. Moving to a managed service can move the architecture decision from enterprise customer to service provider.
limits: Do not equate SAP-certified AMD instances with HANA certification.
Do not infer that Toyota can switch its exact deployment directly to HANA Cloud without a separate application/migration assessment.
No revenue share establishes how large this protected niche is for Intel.
cases.model_use: Define exactly which deployment classes are sticky and quantify their economic weight before extrapolating a segment margin.

source.type: CSP product announcement with customer tests

observations: Google introduced Xeon6 shapes inside the existing C4 family, allowing existing committed-use discounts to continue.
SAS reported testing improvements and intended production expansion; beloFX reported render tests against older N2/N2D machines.
Deutsche Börse reported lower write latency on C4-LSSD; the improvement includes Titanium SSDs.
cases.status: General availability and named testing; no disclosed ordered volume or fleet adoption share.
cases.inference: Keeping the instance family and commercial commitment can reduce refresh friction. Differentiated instructions and complete-system performance may sustain some willingness to pay.
limits: Prior-generation comparisons do not prove superiority to current AMD/Arm.
Storage improvement must not be assigned wholly to the CPU.
Forward production intent is not a completed sale.
cases.model_use: Useful mechanism evidence, insufficient to set a long-run Intel ASP premium or DCAI margin.

source.type: Joint announcement hosted by direct customer
locators: Custom Xeon6 and AI fabric scope

observations: The parties announced a multiyear, multibillion-dollar co-investment framework covering Intel products and wafers. It included custom Xeon6 on Intel3 and an AI fabric chip on Intel18A.
The release does not disclose a CPU-only dollar split, annual delivery schedule, minimum purchases or pricing. Its risk section explicitly includes noncompletion of contemplated transactions.
cases.status: Substantive announced commercial/development framework, not publicly auditable CPU backlog.
cases.inference: This is stronger evidence of strategic Intel retention than a cloud instance catalog. It is still not equivalent to Garrett awarded program revenue with identifiable timing and economics.
limits: Do not allocate the full framework value to DCAI or confuse AWS Ohio datacenter spending with Intel orders.
Foundry wafer economics and Xeon product economics must remain separate.
cases.model_use: Supports customer relationship duration qualitatively; use no incremental quantified revenue without delivery/commitment evidence.

cross_cutting_mechanisms.name: VM live-migration compatibility

sources.locator: Does EVC allow AMD and Intel CPUs to be vMotion compatible?

cross_cutting_mechanisms.fact: Broadcom EVC requires one CPU vendor per compatible cluster. Intel-to-AMD live migration is unsupported; powered-off migration is a different option. Hyper-V also restricts cross-manufacturer running/saved-state moves.
cross_cutting_mechanisms.bull_inference: An installed Intel cluster can have an incremental refresh advantage where downtime is costly.
cross_cutting_mechanisms.bear_boundary: This is switching friction, not impossibility. Planned maintenance, replication, new application deployment or a platform redesign can bypass it. The mechanism is symmetric once a buyer installs AMD.
cross_cutting_mechanisms.model_relevance: Ask how much revenue comes from these deployments and what customers pay to avoid migration. Neither quantity is disclosed by the compatibility rule.

cross_cutting_mechanisms.name: Spend commitments are not CPU purchase contracts

sources.locator: Compute versus EC2 Instance Savings Plans
Compute flexible CUD eligible machine series

cross_cutting_mechanisms.fact: AWS Compute Savings Plans cover different instance families; EC2 Instance Savings Plans are family/region specific. Terms are one or three years, and Savings Plans do not reserve capacity. Google flexible CUDs include C4, C4A and C4D and operate across eligible machine configurations.
cross_cutting_mechanisms.bull_inference: A family-specific commitment can delay a switch because discounts may be stranded.
cross_cutting_mechanisms.bear_boundary: Flexible spend commitments retain the cloud vendor without necessarily retaining the processor vendor. Even a family-specific cloud commitment is not a disclosed Intel CPU order or manufacturer-margin guarantee.
cross_cutting_mechanisms.model_relevance: Do not use cloud contracted revenue or generic multiyear commitments as Intel backlog.

decision_framework.status: Analytical framework, not measured estimates or a fitted forecasting model.
decision_framework.wait_if: Expected disruption, porting, validation and stranded-commitment costs exceed the cost of delayed capacity and any alternative operating advantage, conditional on acceptable Intel delivery timing.
decision_framework.switch_if: Expected value of earlier capacity plus lifecycle operating savings exceeds migration and commitment costs, with acceptable performance and support.
decision_framework.return_if: Intel later delivers a sufficient workload-adjusted total-cost or performance advantage to justify the remaining reallocation cost. Sunk first-port costs should not be counted again if dual-architecture capability is retained.
what_to_measure: Useful work per dollar at required latency and reliability, including software licenses, memory, network, power and operational support.
Time to production and availability of validated replacement capacity.
Incremental engineering and downtime cost, separately from historic sunk migration spending.
Actual repeat deployment share and paid usage after alternatives become available.
CPU manufacturer revenue and costs separately from customer cloud invoices.

counterevidence_that_would_support_40_pe.test: Same-workload repeat purchases after supply normalization
counterevidence_that_would_support_40_pe.required_evidence: Named customers repeatedly selecting paid Xeon capacity after AMD/Arm alternatives are available, with deployment scale or usage share.
counterevidence_that_would_support_40_pe.why_it_matters: Separates preference from lack of alternatives.

counterevidence_that_would_support_40_pe.required_evidence: Comparable CPU ASP or negotiated economics, paired with core counts, capabilities, workload mix and generation.
counterevidence_that_would_support_40_pe.why_it_matters: Separates structural pricing power from richer SKU mix and temporary scarcity.

counterevidence_that_would_support_40_pe.test: Workload economics favor Intel at the assumed premium
counterevidence_that_would_support_40_pe.required_evidence: Production useful-work TCO including licenses, memory, power, utilization, migration and failure costs; current competitor comparison.
counterevidence_that_would_support_40_pe.why_it_matters: Establishes a reason customers voluntarily pay more.

counterevidence_that_would_support_40_pe.required_evidence: Credible share of DCAI sales/profit from certified, specialized or expensive-to-migrate deployments.
counterevidence_that_would_support_40_pe.why_it_matters: A real moat in a small niche cannot by itself support a whole-segment margin.

counterevidence_that_would_support_40_pe.required_evidence: Product revenue, mix, yields, external component costs and allocated expense support the margin after capacity expands.
counterevidence_that_would_support_40_pe.why_it_matters: Customer retention alone does not establish supplier profitability.

benchmark_translation.what_to_copy_from_winners: Choose one falsifiable mechanism and show the complete chain from customer decision to forecast to present valuation. A named repeated deployment and a bounded switching barrier are more useful than a large partnership-logo collection.
benchmark_translation.what_not_to_copy: Do not manufacture contract visibility, normalize every kind of compute into identical cores, or turn a product announcement into backlog. More case studies cannot repair a missing economic mapping.
benchmark_translation.suggested_main_deck_exhibit: One table with protected deployment classes, contestable deployment classes, observed primary evidence, and the specific forecast assumption each can or cannot justify. Keep detailed cases in defense material.
benchmark_translation.first_ten_pages_priority: Replace low-value generic ecosystem descriptions with two opposing concrete cases and the unresolved aggregate-mix test. This improves defensibility without pretending the evidence proves 40%.
